concepts.title: String Theory
concepts.summary: A theoretical framework in physics that explains fundamental forces and particles as tiny vibrating strings rather than point-like dots.
keyPoints: Replaces zero-dimensional point particles with one-dimensional strings.
Vibration patterns determine a particle's physical identity.
Aims to unify Gravity, Electromagnetism, Weak nuclear force, and Strong nuclear force.
history: 1960s: Originally developed to explain the strong nuclear force.
1970s: Physicists realized it includes graviton behavior.
1980s: First Superstring Revolution established five consistent theories.
1995: Edward Witten proposed M-theory, connecting all five into 11 dimensions.

concepts.title: Dark Matter
concepts.summary: An invisible substance that does not emit, absorb, or reflect light, making it detectable primarily through its gravitational interaction with visible matter.
keyPoints: Invisible to standard optical and astronomical telescopes.
Governs cosmic structure by holding galaxies and clusters together.
history: 1933: Fritz Zwicky studied galaxy clusters and proposed missing mass.
1970s: Vera Rubin and Kent Ford observed flat galactic rotation curves.
1980s-2000s: Cosmic Microwave Background measurements confirmed its presence.

concepts.title: Wormholes
concepts.summary: Also known as an Einstein-Rosen bridge, a hypothetical tunnel-like structure connecting two separate points in spacetime.
keyPoints: Consists of two entry/exit mouths connected by a narrow throat.
Relativity equations suggest theoretical possibilities for shortcuts through space and time.
Requires hypothetical exotic matter with negative energy density to remain stable.
history: 1935: Proposed by Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen.
1950s: Coined 'wormhole' by theoretical physicist John Archibald Wheeler.

concepts.title: The Big Bang Theory
concepts.summary: The prevailing cosmological model explaining that the Universe began as an extremely hot singularity approximately 13.8 billion years ago and continues expanding.
keyPoints: Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation provides an afterglow snapshot of the early universe.
Galactic redshift observations demonstrate that galaxies are moving away from each other.
Light element abundances match nucleosynthesis predictions.
history: 1949: Fred Hoyle coined the term 'Big Bang' during a BBC radio broadcast.
1965: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the CMB.

concepts.title: Quasars
concepts.summary: Extremely luminous active galactic nuclei powered by supermassive black holes consuming surrounding celestial matter.

concepts.title: Spaghettification
concepts.summary: The vertical stretching and horizontal compression of objects into long, thin shapes caused by extreme tidal gravitational forces near a black hole.

concepts.title: Pulsars
concepts.summary: Highly magnetized rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation out of their magnetic poles.

concepts.title: Supernova
concepts.summary: A powerful and luminous stellar explosion occurring during the last evolutionary stages of a massive star.

concepts.title: Stars
concepts.summary: Luminous spheroids of plasma held together by their own gravity, generating heat and light via nuclear fusion.

concepts.title: Planets
concepts.summary: Large celestial bodies orbiting stars that possess sufficient mass for self-gravity to form a rounded shape.

concepts.title: Nebulas
concepts.summary: Interstellar clouds of dust, hydrogen, helium, and ionized gases that frequently serve as star-forming nurseries.

concepts.title: Black Holes
concepts.summary: Regions of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, including light and radiation, can escape.

funFacts: A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.
Neutron stars can spin hundreds of times per second.
One million Earths could fit inside the Sun.
The footprints on the Moon will last millions of years.
There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on Earth.
